item.title: Geologists uncover evidence of a missing Late Cretaceous magmatic arc in northwestern Iran
item.description: Mountains preserve evidence of ancient oceans, moving continents and tectonic processes that have shaped Earth over millions of years. Later deformation, erosion and burial, however, can obscure important parts of this geological record. An international research team led by Istanbul Technical University (ITU) has identified evidence of a previously unrecognized Late Cretaceous continental magmatic arc in northwestern Iran. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Hamilton was in her early thirties when she led the team of software engineers that powered NASA's Apollo missions. She later said, "There was no choice but to be pioneers." Yet another in the long line of pioneers (Henrietta Swan Leavitt, Vera C. Rubin, and countless others) who proved that women were just as good if not better than their male counterparts. Meanwhile, today's conservatives are… Fuente: NPR.

item.title: Food testing reveals how diet can add to exposure to 'forever chemicals'
item.description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)—a vast family of chemicals used largely for their nonstick, water-repellent and grease-resistant properties—are called "forever chemicals" because of their remarkable resistance to degradation. They are now ubiquitous in our environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Three quantum-inspired cores leave opposite fingerprints on the ringing of black holes
item.description: Every black hole hides a question at its center. Einstein's theory predicts that whatever falls in is crushed into a singularity, a point of infinite density where the theory itself breaks down. Most physicists expect quantum gravity to replace that point with something finite. But the center lies hidden behind the horizon. How could we ever learn what is there? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
item.description: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week. It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: NASA advances LISA mission contributions with new test telescope
item.description: NASA has taken the next step in the process of developing a new all-glass telescope for the LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) mission, a space observatory designed to detect ripples in space-time called gravitational waves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plant-bacteria partnership reveals how roots access iron locked in soil
item.description: A new study led by Paul Schulze-Lefert from the Max Planck Institute for Plant Breeding Research in Cologne, in collaboration with Ricardo F.H. Giehl at the Leibniz Institute of Plant Genetics and Crop Plant Research in Gatersleben, revealed how Arabidopsis plants adapt their chemical communication with the bacterial root microbiota to maximize the acquisition of bio-unavailable iron from acidic or calcareous soils. The study is now published in Cell. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Adjustable nanosensors turn water pressure into fluorescent signals, with stiffness shaping sensitivity
item.description: A novel nanovesicle-based platform developed at Institute of Science Tokyo can measure hydrostatic pressure by converting pressure-induced molecular changes into fluorescence signals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fluorescent imaging tracks metabolism of cells in real time
item.description: Cornell researchers have designed a new, faster form of two-photon fluorescence imaging for observing cell metabolism in real time, a method that could enable quicker screening of new therapeutic treatments. The findings were published Sept. 4 in Science Advances. The co-lead authors are former postdoctoral researcher Lu Ling, Ph.D. '20, and doctoral student Jack Crowley, M.S. '22. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation—it functions as an extension of school violence, say researchers
item.description: A new study of 4,200 adolescents revealed that cyberbullying rarely occurs in isolation; it almost always functions as an extension of physical and verbal aggression already present in the school environment. The study, conducted at the Federal University of São Paulo (Unifesp) in Brazil, mapped students' involvement in bullying and found that the lines between victims and perpetrators often blur in a cycle of violence spanning both the physical and digital worlds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What a swordfish washing up on British Columbia's coast says about our changing oceans
item.description: Filmmaker and outdoorsperson Quinn Barabash recently made headlines when he found a swordfish carcass nearly two meters (6.6 feet) long on the remote shores of Haida Gwaii in northern British Columbia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nightjar wings reveal a trade-off between hunting slowly and traveling far
item.description: The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nocturnal migratory bird that travels between Europe and southern Africa each year. However, its wings are not only used for long-distance journeys. When hunting insects, the nightjar must be able to slow down, turn sharply and fly at low speeds. Researchers at Lund University have now shown how this trade-off is reflected in the bird's flight mechanics. The study is published in the journal PLOS Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genetic analysis reveals that some specialty coffee seeds do not match their commercial identity
item.description: Genetic analysis revealed that several seeds from a batch sold as Sidra were not, in fact, Sidra; their genetic profile was closer to that of Batian, a Kenyan variety. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: How does AI affect our engagement at work?
item.description: AI is being integrated into our work at a growing rate. Andreas Bergqvist, a Ph.D. student at the Department of Information Technology, has teamed up with colleagues to investigate how AI, automation and robotization affect work engagement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Discovery marks the first detection of variable water clouds outside of the solar system
item.description: A Jupiter-sized world just 7.5 light-years away is cloudy, chemically complex and, it turns out, more like home than anyone expected. Using the James Webb Space Telescope, Brittany Miles, assistant astronomer at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory, led a team that spent 11 hours staring at WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, collecting a spectrum of its light every 15 minutes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Seeks US Industry Plans for Commercial Space Stations
item.description: NASA is advancing American leadership in space by taking the next step toward a future where commercial space stations lead the way in low Earth orbit. On Friday, the agency released its final Request for Proposals inviting industry to submit plans for the next generation of commercial space stations. “In alignment with the President’s National […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: 'Mix-and-match' material's properties can be tuned by changing its metallic 'recipe'
item.description: Scientists have created a new family of materials whose behavior can be tuned by changing their metallic "recipe"—opening new possibilities for uses including gas storage and sensing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are analytics making pro sports less fun? Fans and analysts remain divided
item.description: Today, the discussions of sports analytics in the 2011 movie "Moneyball" often seem quaint. The idea of a team using data to find players who may be more valuable than meets the eye (and less expensive) no longer surprises anyone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New sensing method expands label-free particle detection beyond sensor surfaces
item.description: Finding a single cancer cell in a tube of blood is a bit like finding a needle in a haystack. As researchers seek to detect ever-smaller and rarer targets, from viruses to circulating tumor cells in blood, the demand for ultrasensitive, robust sensors that are practical for real-world samples continues to grow. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI reveals how coating thickness changes the link between surface roughness and pitting resistance
item.description: Localized pitting corrosion can cause sudden failure in aluminum components even when overall corrosion rates are low. Steam coating offers a water-vapor-based route to protective boehmite films, but processing simultaneously changes film thickness, surface morphology, crystallinity and substrate defects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Strong magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to grow beyond the Chandrasekhar limit
item.description: When a dying star runs out of fuel and sheds its outer layers, its remaining core can become an approximately Earth-sized, extremely dense stellar remnant called a white dwarf. For a white dwarf that is not strongly rotating or magnetized, there is a well-known upper mass limit of about 1.4 times the mass of the sun, known as the Chandrasekhar limit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Confidence in a relationship's future is linked to feelings of romantic security
item.description: Feeling secure in a relationship is not only about how people connect with their partners today. It may also depend on how confident they are that the relationship will continue into the future. Feelings of closeness, trust and connection, together with a sense that the relationship is stable and has a future, can shape how people experience their romantic relationships. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: México: una familia gazatí forja una nueva vida en su país de acogida gracias a la cocina
item.description: Dejarlo todo para reconstruir su vida en otro continente. Eso es lo que se ha visto obligada a hacer esta familia gazatí para huir de la guerra que azota al enclave palestino desde hace tres años. En México, se ganan la vida dando a conocer la gastronomía de su país de origen. Esta es la historia. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Researchers call for national consortium to battle agriculture cyber threats
item.description: The threat of cyberattacks against American agriculture and food systems is growing, and Washington State University researchers are helping to lead a call for a national consortium of land-grant universities to study and combat the threat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum chip holds multiple photons at once, opening path to scalable memory
item.description: For highly fragile quantum information systems, the ability to store quantum information is vital—but also challenging. Quantum information is transported in particles of light called photons, which often must be temporarily paused (or "stored") while other, slower quantum operations catch up. This storage must be performed on microchips as small as 1 centimeter (0.4 inches)—a distance covered by light in a few trillionths of a second. Storing photons for a microsecond would represent a massive leap forward for the capabilities of quantum chips. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Demonstrates Next-Generation Heat Shield Technologies
item.description: NASA is testing heat shields that can keep astronauts safe as they return from missions to the Moon and Mars in an unusual way: by taking out the trash. When Northrop Grumman 24th cargo resupply mission for NASA undocked from the International Space Station, it carried a fleet of 12 small, experimental capsules designed to […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Tara Friesen

item.title: Kīlauea's swelling summit helps scientists forecast lava fountain eruptions
item.description: Episodic lava fountaining is a rare volcanic behavior in which repeated, hours-long bursts of molten lava and gas are spewed from volcanic vents, with quiet pauses lasting days to weeks between episodes. These lava fountains have been observed in active volcanoes in places like Hawaii, Iceland and Italy, but researchers still do not fully understand what starts, sustains or stops these individual fountain episodes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: African antelopes spreading in New Mexico: How far could they go under climate change?
item.description: Majestic African antelopes known as gemsbok have been roaming the U.S. Southwest since their introduction in the 1960s and 1970s. Brought to New Mexico as a game species for hunting, gemsbok quickly settled in, expanding more than 100 kilometers (62 miles) from their introduction point. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers say that's due to their exceptional adaptations to arid conditions, which they predict will dramatically expand under climate change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why faculty diversity at universities still lags far behind the changing demographics of college students
item.description: U.S. colleges and universities have long struggled to increase the racial diversity of their faculty. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some climate tipping points are being studied far more than others
item.description: Parts of Earth's climate system can change abruptly once warming pushes them beyond critical thresholds. The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, the Amazon rainforest, coral reefs and major ocean currents are all among the systems containing potential climate tipping points. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Data centers make heat all year long—here's how the ground can hold onto it until winter
item.description: You have probably noticed it on a hot summer day: A basement feels cool even when the air outside is baking. The ground does not heat up and cool down as fast as the air does. A few hundred feet down, it stays close to the local yearly average all year, which can be around 50 degrees Fahrenheit (10 degrees Celsius). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Almost 75% of buildings in Gaza damaged or destroyed since October 7, 2023: An Analysis
item.description: Using satellite data, researchers at Oregon State University find around 75% of the all buildings in Gaza are either damaged or destroyed since October 7, 2023. Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: The oil market that sets today's gas prices was invented in western Pennsylvania
item.description: The fall of 2026 is a moment when energy takes center stage, as geopolitics unfolding far away shows up in Americans' everyday lives. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How plant enzymes learned to tell mirror-image molecules apart
item.description: Many naturally occurring molecules such as menthol or limonene exist in two mirror-image forms, known as enantiomers, that look almost identical but can differ greatly in smell, taste or effect on the body. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Investor perspective prompts auditors to rate CEO misconduct as more significant
item.description: When thinking like investors, auditors are significantly more likely to rate corporate leaders' crimes as material concerns for the investing public, according to new Poole research. In their professional capacities, the study finds, auditors tend to rate executive lapses as less material to their firms' financial performance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny marine microbe sheds new light on how little genetic machinery a cell needs to survive
item.description: Scientists have discovered a previously unknown microorganism that has the smallest genome ever found and may be able to replicate and express its own genetic information. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-responsive inks could make tattoos visible on demand, but safety remains unproven
item.description: A team of engineers has designed a new line of multicolored tattoo inks that switch on and off with different kinds of light. Described in a study published in Matter & Light, the technology could one day help people hide their tattoos when they have an important business meeting. They could even doodle on their own skin using a simple laser pointer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light reads electron spins inside porous crystals, opening path to quantum chemical sensors
item.description: University of Glasgow researchers are part of an international collaboration that could lead to a new generation of quantum sensors. The team, which included researchers from the University of Tokyo, University of Glasgow, University of Sheffield and Kobe University, has for the first time used light to read out the magnetic spin of electrons trapped inside a porous crystalline material known as a metal-organic framework (MOF). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New auditing rules are curbing international money moves, study suggests
item.description: A new study suggests that expanded financial audit reporting is having a significant impact on the behavior of multinational corporations. Specifically, the study finds that requiring more detailed analysis in financial audits appears to be curbing the corporate practice of shifting money internationally to pay less in taxes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Broken bones in ancient homes shed new light on Viking violence
item.description: Fragmented bones and skull pieces found in hearths, beneath floors and in other domestic settings in early Scandinavian settlement sites are providing fresh insights into Iron Age and Viking Age violence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From bogong moths to Christmas beetles—how to slow down and spot more insects
item.description: Millions of people worldwide watched as the Sydney Olympics came to a close in 2000. Meanwhile, thousands of bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) were airborne, making their annual migration to the Australian Alps. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrafast core-level spectroscopy reveals elusive precursors of exciton condensation in quantum materials
item.description: Many fascinating phases in quantum materials emerge when electrons, atoms and other microscopic components begin to act collectively. But these phases do not necessarily appear out of nowhere when a material crosses a transition temperature. Before long-range order develops, microscopic fluctuations can already be present. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Canada's settlement services are going digital. AI should support workers, not replace them
item.description: Artificial intelligence is no longer just a technology-sector issue. It's transforming how public services are organized and delivered, including settlement services for immigrants and newcomers in Canada. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Where does Earth's nitrogen go? Two atoms offer a clue
item.description: Nitrogen is one of life's building blocks, but it's only helpful in the right amounts. Too much nitrogen in water, for example, can lead to poor water quality and the gradual death of aquatic organisms. Microbes remove nitrogen from water by converting it to a gas that escapes into the atmosphere. But scientists have difficulty determining how much nitrogen is removed this way. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cosmic House of Mirrors
item.description: Galaxies warp and multiply as if in a house of mirrors in this image from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope released on Sept. 29, 2026. The brilliant golden galaxies seen here are part of a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies bunched together on one side of the image, however, are not actually […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: My son goes to the gym a lot. How can I tell if this is healthy or a sign something is wrong?
item.description: A teenage boy goes to the gym several times a week. He takes protein powder and watches what he eats carefully. He talks about being "ripped" or "jacked." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SPHEREx spots menagerie of brown dwarfs with atmospheric water and methane
item.description: NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the universe, Epoch of Reionization, and ices Explorer) space telescope is shedding light on brown dwarfs, celestial objects that blur the line between stars and exoplanets. New findings published in The Astrophysical Journal show that these dark and cloudy worlds have chemically rich atmospheres not unlike the giant planets in our own solar system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Week in images: 05-09 October 2026 Discover our week through the lens Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: AI turns bodycam footage into text. Can it keep the speakers straight?
item.description: Turning people into frogs—and back into princes—is the stuff of fairy tales. But back in January 2026, this fate befell a Heber City, Utah, police officer when AI accidentally cast the spell. Transcription software picked up the dialogue from "The Princess and the Frog" playing at the scene where the police encounter was unfolding. When AI software used the recording to draft the report, it mistook the movie dialogue for part of the encounter and claimed the officer had turned into a frog while on duty. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Offering alcohol-free beer on tap boosts pub choices while keeping revenues intact, new study shows
item.description: Simple changes to pub environments can encourage drinkers to choose alcohol-free options without harming profits, according to new research from the University of York. The study, published in Drug and Alcohol Review, evaluated how introducing alcohol-free (AF) beer through three sequential behavioral "nudges" influenced consumer habits and revenues across three distinct U.K. pubs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research reveals surprising link in ocean carbon cycle: Swimming sea cucumbers
item.description: New MBARI research has revealed that the sea cucumber Pelagothuria natatrix plays an important and unexpected role in the ocean's carbon cycle. In a new article published in the journal Ecology, senior scientist Bruce Robison reports that this unique swimming sea cucumber is a prominent member of the midwater community in the Galápagos Islands, intercepting carbon sinking to the deep seafloor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unos astrónomos de Harvard han detectado una histórica señal de radio en el exoplaneta Beta Pictoris b
item.description: Por primera vez, unos científicos han detectado ondas de radio procedentes de un planeta fuera de nuestro Sistema Solar. A menudo, la detección de ondas de radio en el espacio se relaciona con la vida extraterrestre inteligente . Pero no te emociones pensando en eso. En este caso no tiene nada que ver. La medición se ha hecho en el exoplaneta Beta Pictoris b y, si bien es cierto que no está relacionada con alienígenas, sí que tiene otras connotaciones interesantes. Auroras extrasolares . En realidad, no se ha localizado una onda de radio, sino una emisión constante. Gracias al radiotelescopio… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Superconducting circuit links smaller photon groups into larger entangled states
item.description: Quantum computers, computer systems that leverage the laws of quantum mechanics, store and process information using qubits (i.e., quantum bits). In many quantum computers, qubits are linked via entanglement, a quantum mechanical effect that connects particles in such a way that their shared state cannot be described as separate, independent states. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese researchers make Arctic-to-Antarctic call using rival to Musk’s Starlink
item.description: Polar researchers have used a would-be Chinese rival to Elon Musk’s Starlink to make a satellite video call between the Arctic and Antarctic – the first publicly reported test of the Guowang constellation. The call highlights the growing capabilities of the country’s satellite constellations, according to state media. Beijing has been accelerating the development of its low-Earth-orbit constellations in recent years, particularly as the US-based Starlink showed its wartime value by helping... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Liu Zhen

item.title: YouTube overtakes TV as top source of political news, study finds
item.description: The Center for the Creator Economy at Syracuse University—the nation's first academic center dedicated to the advancement of interdisciplinary academics, independent research, policy engagement and support for creator-based ventures—today released the findings from its inaugural industry Flash Report. Published monthly, these reports examine the issues creators, brands and audiences are talking about right now. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hace un millón de años, los humanos venían a este lugar de Tarragona como quien va al supermercado. Los arqueólogos siguen encontrando cosas
item.description: En La Canonja, a pocos kilómetros de Tarragona, hay un yacimiento que lleva dos décadas dando que hablar: el Barranc de la Boella . El IPHES-CERCA lo excava de forma sistemática desde 2007. Resulta interesante por varios motivos. Para empezar, por su antigüedad: sus herramientas de piedra y sus restos de fauna rondan el millón de años. En segundo lugar, porque el equipo defiende que ahí aparece por primera vez en Europa el Achelense , la tecnología de las hachas de mano. Todo eso ya da para un buen documental. Sin embargo, los investigadores insisten en un matiz todavía más potente: los… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: How much noise should we put up with? London and Copenhagen have different answers
item.description: Traffic, trains, nightlife—in cities everywhere, there is a near-constant background hum that most people simply get used to. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rocket Report: A rare Falcon 9 scrub; is it just about Vulcan's time to shine?
item.description: "I can say we’re weeks away from launching on Vulcan." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Are autistic suspects likely to be disadvantaged in forensic interviews?
item.description: A new study led by Flinders University finds both autistic and nonautistic suspects may be judged more harshly if any idiosyncratic behaviors in interviews stray beyond what observers consider normal. The research also undermines the widely held perspective—referred to as the "double empathy hypothesis"—that autistic people can better "read" differing intentions and motivations in other autistic people than nonautistic people can. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Only one workout helped older adults lose fat and keep muscle
item.description: A six-month study suggests that high-intensity interval training (HIIT) may offer older adults a powerful advantage: losing body fat while keeping their muscle. Unlike moderate-intensity workouts, which led to a small loss of lean muscle, HIIT preserved it while also improving body composition around the waist. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: An Instafamous giant water lily is confirmed as a new species — and critically endangered
item.description: A chance sighting of photos on Instagram, then a five-day expedition, including a last-minute, late-night detour in a Colombian rainforest — that’s what it took for researchers to confirm a new-to-science species of giant water lily. The plant has such large leaves the researchers could also spot it from space, according to a new study. […] Fuente: Mongabay.
item.dc:creator: Hayat Indriyatno

item.title: Scientists find hidden materials that could improve batteries and solar fuels
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden world of “in-between” materials that briefly form as chemical ingredients are heated, revealing structures that conventional methods can miss. Among the discoveries is a previously unknown form of bismuth vanadate, a material widely studied for using sunlight to help produce clean hydrogen. The new version has a different atomic structure and interacts with light in a strikingly different way, potentially opening new possibilities for solar fuels, catalysts, and electronics. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Walking through flames: Orangutans rescued in Indonesia fires
item.description: The orangutan clings to the top of a mostly leafless tree in Indonesia's portion of Borneo as waves of thick smoke from the forest fires burning below waft over her. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bacteria turn a virus’ own weapon against it
item.description: Researchers have uncovered a new way bacteria detect viral attacks: a virus-produced enzyme cuts a bacterial sensor protein, triggering a self-destructing immune response. The discovery could lead to more effective phage therapies against antibiotic-resistant bacteria and provide insight into ancient immune mechanisms shared with humans. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Seals and sea lions get their hearing tested at Australia Zoo
item.description: Scientists in Australia trained sea lions and seals to respond to a hearing test for research into how the marine mammals are affected by human-made noise. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fired OpenAI researchers say they were let go for 'prioritising safety'
item.description: The AI firm instead claims the researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive information. Publicado también por: BBC News - Business. Fuente: BBC News - World.

item.title: Malaysia closes schools in capital, parts of country due to haze
item.description: Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country Friday as haze from fires in neighboring Indonesia again pushed local air quality to some of the world's worst levels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fish may look fine in urban waters but their genes tell a different story
item.description: Blue damselfish, with their striking blue hue, are easy to spot, even along Okinawa's heavily urbanized coastlines. But while abundant, their gene activity reveals a hidden cost to living in human-impacted environments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Molecular movie' finally reveals how penicillin is made
item.description: Researchers from the University of Oxford and international collaborators have revealed previously unseen rapid chemical stages in the formation of β-lactam antibiotics like penicillin, offering insights that can support future antibiotic development. The findings have been published in Nature Catalysis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D genome 'entanglement' may explain how cephalopods evolved complex brains
item.description: Octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, collectively known as coleoid cephalopods, have evolved exceptionally large and elaborately structured nervous systems capable of complex behaviors such as problem-solving and rapid camouflage. A new study by scientists at the University of Vienna suggests that the origins of this complexity may lie not just in the genes themselves, but in how the genome is organized in 3D. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 9-billion-year-old signal could help explain dark energy
item.description: A Canadian radio telescope has detected the faint glow of hydrogen from billions of years ago using only its own observations, proving a long-awaited way to map the distant universe can actually work. CHIME can use this hydrogen signal to trace how matter is spread across space and measure how the universe has expanded over time, offering a powerful new way to investigate dark energy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: OpenAI defends decision to fire researchers: 'These decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out'
item.description: OpenAI has defended its decision to fire three safety researchers for what the AI lab has described as a "significant breach of trust" Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: A quantum prediction from 1931 just came to life
item.description: Nearly a century after physicist Hans Bethe predicted them, scientists have created and directly observed unusual quantum states known as “Bethe strings” in an ultracold gas. By cooling cesium atoms to near absolute zero and trapping them in thousands of tiny one-dimensional tubes, researchers were able to make groups of atoms bind together without ordinary chemical bonds. These strange clusters could contain six or more particles and even collide with one another without falling apart. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Four astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
item.description: SpaceX brought France's Sophie Adenot and fellow astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and Andrey Fedyaev back to Earth on Thursday after an eight-month mission on board the International Space Station that saw Adenot become the first French woman to walk in space. Publicado también por: France 24 - English. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El James Webb ha encontrado los restos de choques violentos entre mundos en formación. Y son más comunes de lo que creíamos
item.description: Hace años, el telescopio espacial Spitzer encontró algo curioso en torno a unas pocas estrellas jóvenes. Se trataba de discos de polvo inusualmente calientes, muy diferentes a los discos de escombros convencionales que pueden quedar como remanente después del nacimiento de estas. Para poder estudiar el origen de estos fenómenos, bautizados como discos de escombros extremos, era necesario detectar más casos. Sin embargo, el Spitzer se “jubiló” sin llegar a lograrlo. Por suerte, el James Webb sí que ha dado un gran paso en ese aspecto, aportando datos que han permitido a los científicos… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: firm uses 3D-printed tiles to restore coral reefs
item.description: In 2014, a University of Hong Kong research team watched two years of reef restoration work collapse in Sai Kung. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department had asked the researchers to speed up coral recovery. Cement structures were placed on the seabed and coral began to grow. But as the colonies became larger, they became unstable. “They have no roots,” said Vriko Yu Pik-fan, then a doctoral student on the project. “The bigger they got, the less stable they were.” That failure... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find
item.description: Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle. But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered. Continue reading... Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
item.description: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists create new statewide surface geologic map of Nebraska
item.description: A new academic paper by Paul Hanson and Matthew Joeckel of the Conservation and Survey Division in the University of Nebraska–Lincoln's School of Natural Resources contains a brief phrase—"new linework"—that looks innocuous but carries enormous meaning. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global analysis reveals how armed conflict erodes farmland and potential food production
item.description: Armed conflict accelerates cropland loss, and the effects can persist for years after conflict begins and vary substantially with conflict severity and social conditions, according to a new study published in Nature Food on Sept. 24. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: October’s night sky is full of cosmic tricks and treats
item.description: October’s skies are packed with celestial surprises, from Jupiter disappearing behind the Moon to two meteor showers lighting up the darkness. NASA highlights four must-see events, including shooting stars from Halley’s Comet and a glowing Hunter’s Moon just before Halloween. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nearly 30,000 people tested quit-smoking methods. One stood out
item.description: Nicotine e-cigarettes appear to help more smokers quit than patches, gum, and several other common approaches, according to a major review of 80 clinical trials. Researchers say regulated vaping products are not risk-free, but may be a significantly less harmful alternative for people who would otherwise continue smoking. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Research shows how AI and mixed reality can enhance police work
item.description: How can AI provide police officers with better support in complex situations? In an interdisciplinary collaboration, researchers in police research and computing science at Umeå University have explored the opportunities and risks associated with using AI-based interactive systems in police work. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Most trading card packs hide the odds of winning rare cards, study finds
item.description: Pokémon, sports and other physical trading and collectible cards have been around for decades but have surged in popularity since COVID. These cards are usually obtained through gambling-like packs containing random cards. Most packs do not offer any highly desirable cards, but a few packs will. Consumers, often including children, therefore buy many packs in the hope of obtaining rare chase cards. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, scientist who worked on Nasa's Apollo programme, dies
item.description: Margaret Hamilton, an American scientist known for her work on NASA's Apollo program, has recently passed away. She played a crucial role in developing the software for the Apollo missions, ensuring safe lunar landings. Hamilton's contributions to computing have been recognized widely, including the awarding of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Her work not only advanced technology but also inspired future generations in science and engineering. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Introducing LGBT stories linked to more inclusive attitudes in primary schools
item.description: Can literature foster greater acceptance of LGBT people among elementary school students? This is the core question behind a study conducted by researchers Guillermo Soler, María Ribes and José Rovira-Collado from the Language and Literature Didactics area of the Department of Teaching Innovation and Training at the University of Alicante (UA). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists tested 5 natural compounds on cancer cells. One stood out
item.description: Five natural compounds, including curcumin and berberine, were tested for their effects on cancer cells and healthy muscle cells. All disrupted cancer cell energy production and pushed many of the cells into a non-dividing state, with curcumin producing the strongest overall effect. Curcumin also showed a relatively favorable safety profile, while some other compounds caused more toxicity. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Study documents beef industry group's early efforts to counter climate concerns
item.description: A leading U.S. beef industry trade association knew by 1989 that cattle contributed to global warming but focused its response on protecting consumer demand through public relations, according to a new study that examined a decade of industry records. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Only 9% of major companies use biodiversity indicators, study finds
item.description: Biodiversity indicators can help companies make more sustainable decisions. But only 9% of the world's largest companies in sectors with a major impact on biodiversity use such indicators, according to a new study from Lund University. The researchers also show that different indicators can lead to different conclusions and present seven recommendations for how they should be used. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The genetic switch behind the butterfly's enhanced visual world of color
item.description: Many insects see the world through hundreds of tiny lenses that are grouped together in a visual organ known as the compound eye. Behind each lens sits a cluster of eight light-detecting cells arranged in a pattern that scientists believe has existed for hundreds of millions of years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cows deliver healthy calves without embryonic protein long thought essential for pregnancy
item.description: For decades, scientists have believed that a protein called interferon tau (IFNT) is indispensable for pregnancy in cattle. Produced by the early embryo, it was thought to signal its presence to the mother and prevent the hormonal changes that would otherwise end the pregnancy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stratospheric winds can warn of extreme energy demand in Europe
item.description: A breakdown of normal polar winds in winter raises the chance of extreme cold—and a resulting spike in energy demand—in Europe, new research shows. Normally, strong and stable westerly winds circle high above the Arctic in the winter, in what is known as the "stratospheric polar vortex." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chance Instagram sighting leads to discovery of rare giant water lily in Colombia
item.description: A new paper published in the journal Phytotaxa describes a new species in the genus Victoria, the Colombian giant water lily (Victoria colombiana). With only three other known species in the genus, V. colombiana joins the pantheon of nature's giants with pads measuring up to 2 meters (6.6 feet) across. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bees struggle to smell flowers when air pollutants combine
item.description: Bees, moths and other pollinating insects have a harder time smelling flowers in polluted air, according to research led by the University of Reading. Scientists analyzed 22 experimental studies on how the air pollutants ozone and nitrogen oxides (NOx) affect pollinators. Both pollutants make it harder for pollinators to find flowers by breaking down or altering the scents that flowers give off. Fuente: Phys.org.
